newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU summit to get look at possible new treaty.
newsitem.headline: EU summit to get look at possible new treaty.

text.p: The European Union's next big idea -- to create by 2001 an area of freedom, security and justice that ensures the free movement of people -- is likely to be the focus of attention at the European Council on Friday.

Host Ireland is to deliver a progress report on negotiations on a new EU treaty which calls for the bloc to consider such an area as a way of fighting crime and bringing citizens closer to the 15-member Union.

Britain, the Netherlands and others will be intensely wary of some aspects of the idea, but an open row at the Dublin summit is unlikely. The report is couched in such a way that the leaders will be able to endorse it without actually having to come out in favour of anything in it.
It leaves for later -- during the six months before the next EU summit in June in Amsterdam that is expected to agree a new treaty -- many of the most contentious issues facing the bloc.

These includes extending Qualified Majority Voting, the reform of EU institutions and "flexibility" -- whether countries should be able to integrate faster than others using EU structures and institutions.

Overall, however, the draft shows the direction in which the majority of countries are heading -- towards closer cooperation in crime fighting, an employment chapter, stronger Common Foreign and Security Policy links, and a true border-free Europe with common asylum and immigration policies.
The last idea is an attention-grabbing policy, following on from previous landmark EU decisions to create a single market, then a single currency.

It was endorsed on Monday when French President Jacques Chirac and German Chancellor Helmut Kohl proposed at a pre-summit meeting in Nurembourg the gradual harmonising of EU drugs and crime legislation.

The two leaders' call for what they called a European judicial area was wrapped up as a Franco-German proposal, but Brussels diplomats noted its similarity to one of the main elements already contained in a draft treaty unveiled last week.

Indeed, Kohl and Chirac offered little at their meeting that was not in the draft treaty, signalling that neither is likely to risk disrupting the summit in Dublin on Friday and Saturday with demands for a hefty debate on European integration.
This had been something of a concern to the Irish presidency following an outburst at last Friday's General Affairs Council by French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette.
Ireland calls on its fellow EU members to consider a project to create "perhaps by January 1, 2001, an area of freedom, security and justice in which the free movement of person would be ensured".

Although some of the motivation for the project is the desire by EU leaders to make their bloc meaningful to its citizens -- by guaranteeing minumum human rights, for example -- the fight against crime is also a major driving force.
Ireland, Germany and France have pushed the fight against drugs and organised crime high up the EU agenda and are expected to make much in Dublin of a common struggle against crime.

In a letter to Irish Prime Minister John Bruton, Kohl and Chirac said: "Faced with the growing threat that international organised crime, the drug mafia and terrorism are imposing on our citizens and institutions...we must be able to create a common European judicial area capable of guaranteeing at the same time a greater freedom of movement and more security for our citizens."
The idea, however, is not uniformly welcome in EU capitals.

Britain, its Conservative government paralysed by an internal debate over Europe, is likely to resist to the end any lifting of its internal borders, the pooling of judicial responsibilities and a common immigration policy.

The Netherands, which takes over from Ireland as president for six months on January 1, is also wary of attempts to force it to change its liberal marijuana laws -- which it says work and which Paris says open France to an influx of Dutch-bought drugs.
